opening.headline: It explains why the operation continues using the previous version after changing the model version through version referencing and alias promotion.
body: Even if a new model version is registered and verified, operations will not change if the service directly references the version number. Upgrades and rollbacks are tied to code deployments.

In this class, we examine the lifecycle of Unity Catalog model registry, the behavior of aliases, and the promotion and rollback paths between alias and stage methods. We then discuss case studies involving hardcoding and rollback after promotion.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the alias promotion in Unity Catalog model registry
Can distinguish between version reference methodology and upgrade/rollback paths

screens.title: I changed the version, but the operation uses the previous version.
screens.lead: Let's examine the scenario where increasing the model version does not change the results. Check the scene to identify what parts are fixed.

paragraphs: The team has registered and validated the new model version 3. They now expected to receive predictions from version 3 in operations. However, the operational service still returns predictions from version 1.

The issue was in the service code. Since the version number was hardcoded when loading the model, the service is not aware of changes to the version stored in the registry. To use the new version, the code must be modified and redeployed.

This issue is about how a model version is referenced, i.e., the model version referencing problem. In this class, we will explain alias promotion in Unity Catalog's model registry and distinguish between promotion and rollback paths when referencing models by version number versus by alias.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Is passing verification equivalent to operating with the new version? Consider this question again at the end of the class.

visual.alt: Version 1, 2, 3 of the model registry, with a fixed arrow pointing to version 1 of the operational service.

screens.outro: First, let's recall our organization's promotion process.

screens.title: Who approves in the promotion process?
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thought process is displayed. Please first think about the answer on your own before clicking it.

items.prompt: Who has the final decision on deploying the model into operations?
items.answer: Many organizations are unclear about who holds the authority for this decision. It could differ among the person who created the model, the person who validated it, and the person operating the service. As will be seen later, the authority to change an alias becomes the point of approval.

items.prompt: Is there a predefined method to roll back to a previous version when a problem occurs?
items.answer: If rollback requires code modifications and redeployment, it will extend downtime. Check whether your system supports rollback through a single operation. This lesson describes such a structure.

items.prompt: Is promotion and deployment configuration change occurring with a single operation by the same user?
items.answer: Then it means that verification and approval are concentrated in one person. If promotion is separated into a distinct operation, it becomes easier to record and control who and when performed the promotion.

screens.outro: Based on the question that comes to mind, let's examine the model lifecycle.

screens.title: Model Lifecycle and Unity Catalog Registry
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to step through the flow of the model learning and being accumulated in the registry.

steps.title: The role of the registry
steps.body: Unity Catalog's model is the hosted version of MLflow Model Registry. It provides centralized access control, auditing, lineage, and search. With all models consolidated in one place, you can easily manage who accesses which models and track the data used for training.

steps.title: Name is a 3-level structure
steps.body: Model names have three parts: `catalog.schema.model`, for example `prod.ml_team.iris_model`. The name tells you which catalog and schema the model belongs to.

steps.title: Permissions required for registration
steps.body: Registering a new model requires `CREATE MODEL` and `USE SCHEMA` on the schema, plus `USE CATALOG` on the catalog. Without these privileges, registration fails even after training finishes.

steps.title: Versions accumulate.
steps.body: When you register learning results, versions accumulate in sequence, such as version 1, 2, 3. Once a version is registered, it becomes an immutable record, so you cannot register the same version number again.

steps.title: The environment is merely structural.
steps.body: Just because a model is listed in the product catalog does not mean that version is receiving operational traffic. The environment reflects only the naming structure; actually, which version is serving is determined by the service's reference configuration. Dividing development, validation, and operations into catalog entries is a structural approach for access control, not an indicator of which version is currently in production. Misunderstanding this distinction leads to the mistaken belief that a deployment is complete simply because a version is listed in production.

screens.outro: Since we've seen the version accumulation structure, let's now look at the alias—which indicates which version is being operated.

screens.title: alias: label indicating the version
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to follow the movement of the Champion badge across version spaces. You can observe how the response version received by the inference service changes at each step.

steps.title: What is an alias?
steps.body: An alias is a label attached to a specific version of a registered model. A label can be moved to another version at any time. A version is a cumulative, immutable record, while an alias is a movable pointer.

steps.title: Champion in version 1
steps.body: If a champion alias is specified in version 1, all inferences referring to the champion use version 1. This is the current state of the operational model.

steps.title: Champion version 2
steps.body: When the verified version 2 is ready, Champion is re-designated to version 2. This action constitutes the promotion. The service code does not change, but the version in the response does.

steps.title: Appearance in reasoning
steps.body: On the reasoning side, the model is loaded using a URI of the form `models:/prod.ml_team.iris_model@Champion`. The difference lies in the fact that aliases are used instead of version numbers.

steps.title: Reflection point
steps.body: When Champion points to a new version, deployment inference automatically uses the new version on the next execution. A serving endpoint can implement a deployment flow that queries the current version via an alias and then updates the endpoint to serve that version. In other words, alias migration does not immediately imply serving updates, and the rollout strategy depends on the service configuration. It is safe to include a step in the procedure to verify which version actually serves responses after promotion.

steps.title: Benefits of aliases
steps.body: Using aliases separates the service code from the model's version history. The model team can freely build and accumulate versions, while the operations team only needs to care about the target pointed to by the alias. The boundaries of responsibility between the two teams become clear, and the scope of change impact is reduced. As promotions become a routine process, improved models can be deployed to production more frequently and safely.

screens.outro: Since we've confirmed the method of promotion using aliases, let's compare the promotion and rollback paths in two different ways.

screens.title: Upgrade and rollback paths: aliases and stage
screens.lead: Select the Status button to compare the promotion and rollback paths for alias mode and stage mode.

states.label: alias method
states.body: In Unity Catalog, promoting an alias to a different version is referred to as promotion. Rolling back to a previous version is called rollback, and the process ends when the Champion is re-designated to the immediately prior version, requiring no changes to service code or deployment files. When promoting an alias, appropriate permissions and approval rules must be designed by environment. Who is authorized to perform the promotion defines the approval gate. It is common to grant broad permissions in development environments and limited permissions in operational environments. Only individuals who have gone through the approval process should be allowed to promote operational aliases.

states.label: stage mode (legacy)
states.body: The legacy workspace model registry uses stage transition methods such as staging, production, and archived. Advancing a version's stage is referred to as promotion. In a workspace with Unity Catalog enabled, users are guided to use Unity Catalog models instead of the legacy procedures. Therefore, when designing new promotion workflows, using aliases is the appropriate approach. If stage-based workflows are already in place, reference is made by determining which version is currently in production. While both approaches share the commonality that promotion involves operations within the registry rather than code deployment, this course designates aliases as the preferred standard. Comparing rollback paths clearly highlights the differences: the alias method simply reassigns the name tag to a previous version, whereas the version number method requires reverting the code and redeploying it.

screens.outro: We have compared both approaches; now let's apply them to a hardcoding scenario.

screens.title: Explanation Example: A Service with Hardcoded Version Number
screens.lead: The instructor explains the process of changing a fixed-version service to be referenced by an alias. Select the right arrow to proceed step by step.

steps.title: The problematic code
steps.body: The service directly references a version number like `models:/prod.ml_team.iris_model/1`. This service always loads version 1, regardless of how the model changes in the registry.

steps.title: Promotion is not reflected
steps.body: Even if the new version 3 passes validation, the service continues to use version 1 until the code is redeployed. While the model team believes they have completed the promotion, operations are reverting to the previous model. This mismatch often goes unnoticed because it proceeds without error messages and is typically discovered only after user complaints arise. Therefore, such silently misaligned structures pose a greater risk.

steps.title: Rollback is also slow.
steps.body: Rollbacks are similar in this regard. To revert to a previous version, the code must be modified and redeployed, which extends downtime. The fundamental issue is that both upgrades and rollbacks are tied to deployment operations.

steps.title: Revision: looks at aliases only
steps.body: The service now only looks at aliases such as `@Champion`. Then, upgrades are completed with a single alias migration. The service code no longer needs to know version numbers. This change is completed with a single deployment, after which all future upgrades can occur without any additional deployment.

steps.title: Approval and Audit Points
steps.body: By granting a small number of users the permission to move aliases and recording the moves, promotion approvals and acknowledgments occur at a single point. Who moved it, when, and to which version becomes the change history.

steps.title: Remaining inspection items
steps.body: Even after modification, there are still items to verify. Check whether the version pointed to by the alias is the intended version, and confirm how the serving endpoint reflects the alias change. Changing the structure and verifying the structure are separate concerns. Additionally, if the alias migration permissions are too broad, even if hardcoded issues are resolved, a new problem may arise allowing anyone to alter the operational model; therefore, review the migration permission design as well.

screens.outro: If the promotion structure has been changed, you should also verify the rollback process in case problems arise.

screens.title: Explanation Example: Anomaly Detection and Rollback After Promotion
screens.lead: After upgrading to version 3, the instructor explains the situation where prediction quality deteriorates. Select the right arrow to proceed in sequence.

steps.title: Case conditions
steps.body: After upgrading Champion to version 3, signals indicating degraded prediction quality have been received. The service is structured to face the `@Champion` alias. The objective is to minimize service disruption while enabling root cause analysis.

steps.title: Step 1: Verify current status
steps.body: Query the version pointed to by Champion to actually verify if it is 3. We must start with a query rather than speculation because someone else might have already moved the alias.

steps.title: Step 2: Rollback
steps.body: Reassign Champion to version 2. No code changes or redeployment are required. Then verify that the next service returns responses from the previous version.

steps.title: Step 3: Preservation of Problem Version
steps.body: Version 3 is retained instead of being deleted for root cause analysis. Separate aliases can be added if needed for differentiation. If the problematic version is removed, the evidence for root cause analysis is also lost.

steps.title: Step 4: Record
steps.body: Records reversed timestamps and reasoning. To avoid repeating the same issues at the next promotion review, this record is essential. The rationale for reversal serves as justification for enhancing the promotion checklist.

steps.title: organizing
steps.body: In this case, the rapid rollback was possible because the service was monitoring the alias. If the version number had been hardcoded in the code, a waiting period for redeployment would have been necessary under the same circumstances. Additionally, leaving the problematic version enabled allowed for root cause analysis, and maintaining records enabled lessons to be learned and applied in future promotions. The three elements—rapid rollback, evidence preservation, and record-keeping—form the safety net of the promotion process.

steps.title: Verification question
steps.body: As we conclude this case, three questions arise for ourselves. Does our service treat aliases as a primary concern? Does modifying code become necessary when handling alias resolution? Who is authorized to relocate aliases, and is this action properly documented? If we can confidently answer all three questions, then the promotion process can be considered stable. If any of these questions remain unanswered, that area becomes a priority for improvement.

screens.title: Key points and reflection
screens.lead: Summarizes the core of the lesson in one go.

paragraphs: In Unity Catalog Model Registry, versions are immutable, accumulating records, and aliases are movable labels that point to a specific version. Operational services must refer to aliases, not version numbers.

Promotion involves moving an alias to a new version, while rollback involves reassigning the alias to a previous version. Both operations can be performed without changing or redeploying the service code. Therefore, the authority to move an alias becomes the approval point.

Going back to the initial question, passing validation and using a new operational version are separate concerns. The alias promotion connects these two. When designing the promotion process, jointly determine who can be promoted, whether migration records are retained, and whether rollback options exist. Once these three aspects are clearly defined, the operational system remains stable even as model versions accumulate. Versions can be freely stacked, but operations are controlled through version labels—this is the key point of today's lesson.

glossary.def: The model version management flow progresses through learning, registration, verification, operation, and rollback.
A mutable label pointing to a version of a registered model. Champion is a typical example.
This determines whether to reference a model by version number or by alias when loading a model.
When problems occur, you restore operation by reassigning the alias to the previous version.
An MLflow registry model named catalog.schema.model that receives access control and lineage.

misconceptions.myth: Registration of a new version is automatically reflected in the operation.
misconceptions.fact: The version indicated by operation is separate. Moving an alias is promotion.

misconceptions.myth: If it is in the product catalog, it receives operational traffic.
misconceptions.fact: The catalog defines only the environment structure; the actual serving target is determined by the reference setting.
You can revert it without changing the code by reassigning the alias to the previous version.

closing.lead: We will summarize the key points of today's class.
points: Version is a growing immutable record, and alias is a movable label.
Promotion is alias migration, and rollback is the process of reverting to a previous version of an alias.
The right to move an alias is exactly the approval point.
closing.reflectionLead: The following question is for your own reflection. Answers will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Our model service refers to either the version number or the alias; who is authorized to modify that reference?

title: Alias promotion and the model lifecycle

checks.q: Version 3 of the iris_model in prod.ml_team has been registered. What can we definitely conclude from this fact?
options: The model in the production catalog is always served at its highest version.
Version 3 is an immutable record, and its operational implementation is separately determined.
Version 3 can be modified to allow re-registration with the same number.
checks.explain: Version is an immutable record with an increasing sequence number, and being listed in the prod catalog merely indicates the environment structure, not actual traffic reception.

wrong.0: You cannot assume traffic based solely on catalog name.
wrong.1: The served version specifies the reference mode, and the highest version is not automatically selected.
wrong.3: Registered versions are immutable and are not rewritten with the same number.

checks.intro: Just learned about the relationship between version and operational reflection. Select something definitely verifiable from the fact that a version has been registered. An unrecorded self-audit.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes. The registered version is an immutable record, and operational rollout is separately defined.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Think again. The existence of a version and the operation of using that version are two different matters.

checks.q: After upgrading to version 3 in a structure where the operating service watches @Champion alias, issues arose. What is the fastest rollback method?
options: Replaces the version number of the service code and redeploys it.
Set Champion to the previous version again
Delete version 3 and re-register it with the same name.
Archives the stage of the legacy registry
checks.explain: Rollback involves reassigning the alias to the previous version, allowing you to revert without modifying the service code or deployment files.

wrong.0: This is a slow approach that is only necessary in a structure where version numbers are fixed in the code.
wrong.2: Deletion results in loss of root cause analysis data and is unnecessary for rollback.
wrong.3: Stage switching is a legacy approach and is not used in Unity Catalog models.

checks.intro: This is a situation where problems arose after promotion within a structure that looks at aliases. Try the fastest approach. An unrecorded self-assessment.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes. Assigning the alias to the previous version is the fastest rollback.
checks.incorrectFeedback: This method is either unnecessarily slow or does not fit well with this structure. Recall again what the alias points to.

checks.q: When upgrade-related predicted quality degradation signals occur, consider the appropriate response in the correct order.
items: This retrieves the actual version that Champion is pointing to.
Redefines Champion to the previous version.
The problem version is retained instead of being deleted for cause analysis.
checks.explain: Check the current state, revert using alias, preserve the problematic version, and record the changes in order.
checks.intro: After a quality degradation signal is received, review the responses in sequence. This is a record-keeping self-check.
checks.correctFeedback: The order is correct: query, rollback, version retention, logging.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The order is incorrect. The current state must be verified first, then reverted, followed by preservation and recording.
